utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cepic, you have a preliminary matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, yesterday I forgot to request admission of some documents. I spoke already with my learned friend Mr. Groome and he will have no objection about that. That is the testimony -- transcript of testimony of VG-13 [Realtime transcript read in error "VG-14"] from Vasiljevic case and information sheet for some witnesses which I'd shown to VG-13 during the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit those.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In transcript is an error, line 9, VG-13, not 14. My pronunciation of English is not perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the pseudonym sheet become exhibit number 2D7; 1D10-0049 will become Exhibit 2D8; 1D10-0149 will become Exhibit 2D9, all under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, the Court has ordered certain protective measures with respect to your identity and your testimony here today, so I will be referring to you as VG-32 during your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that we go into private session briefly before I show the witness the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask the usher to please hand the witness a pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, can I ask that you look at the paper that you've just been handed and ask you is that your name indicated on that sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that your date of birth on that sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that you sign the sheet with your signature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, after the document has been shown to Defence counsel and the Chamber I'd ask that it be admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be admitted as P64 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. I haven't heard it being assigned an exhibit number yet. Is that something we need to do before we proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit will become P64 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, as you can see on the bottom of the pseudonym sheet that you have there are the pseudonyms of two other people who you may refer to in your testimony. I would ask you to please remember to do -- to refer to them by their name. Your Honour, the witness has a considerable amount of evidence to give today. It expedite matters if I were permitted to lead the witness on some background information and some information that is -- I don't believe is in issue in the case, so with the Court's leave I would seek to be able to lead him on his background and some background information about Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That would be -- that will be allowed, but should Defence -- should the Defence team believe that any matter that you raise is a controversial matter, then they are entitled to bring it to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, to expedite matters I'm going to summarise some information that you have provided both in your testimony in the past and in your statements and ask you whether I have recounted that information correctly. With respect to your educational and professional background, is it true that you were born in 1965 in the Visegrad area, you completed your primary education in Visegrad and your secondary education in Sarajevo. In Sarajevo you attended the medical school. While you are not a medical doctor, you did receive training in one of the health professions. You returned to the town of Visegrad where you worked in the health centre there. In 1988, you returned to school to do additional studies in a related or another health care field. Is all of this information correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It is. My apologies, Your Honour. The year 1988 should in fact be 1998, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. With that correction, was the rest of the information correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the spring of 1992, you left Visegrad sometime between the 10th and the 12th of April, 1992, when the conflict broke out in Visegrad. The conflict first broke out in the areas outside of the town of Visegrad but then soon came to the town itself. You did not want to take part in the conflict and were opposed to violence of any kind. Out of concern for your wife and your young family, you decided to leave Visegrad and go to Gorazde; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the spring of '92, were you married and did you have a child?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. I was married with one child, a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how old was your daughter at that stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: This was in -- if -- if you count it from early spring, then she was 20 months old. If late spring, then 22 months old. So under -- just under two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it true that while you were in Gorazde you saw media reports that the Uzice Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army had entered the town and that the town had been secured and that the town authorities had guaranteed the safety of all those who returned to the town regardless of their ethnic background? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was the media used to notify those Visegradians who had left the town that they had a work obligation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you understand that to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: My understanding was, and that's in fact what I did, was that I should go back to the town of Visegrad and report to my workplace at the health centre. I realised that unless I went back to my work I'd lose my job. I did not believe that the war would break out the way it did. I believed that with my return to Visegrad the war would end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've told us that you have returned to Visegrad. Do you remember the approximate dates of when you returned to Visegrad from Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact date. It was roughly two weeks later that I returned to Visegrad. Therefore, sometime on the 25th or 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you returned to Visegrad was the Uzice Corps still occupying the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On your way back to Visegrad did you encounter any check-points?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Other witnesses have testified about what these check-point were, so it may not be necessary for you to go into any great detail about the check-points you went through, but could I ask you to simply tell us approximately how many check-points were you stopped at on your way into Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I was stopped at five check-points. The last check-point, the fifth one, was at the very entry to Visegrad just before the Drina Bridge. If you want me to, I can list the places where I was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe that's necessary at this point. If it becomes relevant perhaps we'll ask you then. Is it true that after your return you did not feel safe because you learned that people of Muslim ethnicity were being required to report to the police station and very often those that reported did not return? Further, on one occasion outside the Visegrad medical centre where you worked you witness a soldier shoot an entire clip of ammunition from his automatic weapon into the air. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did both of these events occur while the Uzice Corps was still in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you personally know some of the people who went to the police station and were not seen again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew quite a few of them. I had been friends with some. With others I knew them as acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you aware of any Muslim houses that were being burned during this period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While the Uzice Corps was present in the town, did you observe any paramilitary groups in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name or names that the group or groups were referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: The groups that were present in the town of Visegrad shared a common name of White Eagles. That's how we referred to them regardless of the group they belonged to. I believe that there were more than one group in Visegrad. There was also mention of there being Seselj's men and Arkan's men too. I also heard at some point that there was a group called Garavi Sokak. So there were several names that circulated in reference to these groups. I'm speaking about that time period and the circumstances prevailing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you know any of the locations in which the paramilitaries used to sleep or use as their headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: One of the locations that was widely known that I had to pass by every day is the Visegrad Hotel, which is right next to the Visegrad bridge on the right-hand side. Every morning I had to go past the hotel on my way to work. There was always a guard standing outside the hotel, sometimes just outside the hotel and at other times on the sidewalk by the road some ten metres away from the hotel. I only knew one of those who was a local. Others were unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Visegrad Hotel, is that also known as the New Hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were stopped by members of a paramilitary group while the Uzice Corps was still in town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe when that happened and what happened in that event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I really don't know the date itself. I know that the Uzice Corps was still present there. As I was on my way back from work, I was stopped. Let me just note that during a period of time the safest way of one to go to work would be to take the car, because it would just take me a moment to get to the other bank of the Drina where I worked, and the same was true for my journey home. However, one day as I was going back from work, I was stopped by two individuals outside the hotel. I think that they treated me properly. They asked me to show them my ID, to open the car boot and then to open the front engine boot. One of them took my ID papers and went into the hotel while the others -- the other ones stayed outside with me. He came back several minutes later, told his colleague, "He's not there," returned my ID to me and told me that I was free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When he said, "He's not there," what did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: My logic was that if he took my ID and went into the hotel, most probably he had a list in the hotel and went there to check whether my name was on it. As he went back and said, "He's not there," he must not have found my name on the list. I don't know why else he would have taken my identity card.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After that date did you ever drive your car again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No, I never drove to work from that day on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know the name -- or a person by the name of Dr. Safet Sahilovic? Was he a colleague of yours at the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Let me just make a correction. Safet Zejnilovic. Yes, I know him very well. We are very good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to spell his last name so the record records it correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Safet Zejnilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Dr. Zejnilovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. I know very well what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe that to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Dr. Safet Zejnilovic was in the town of Visegrad before the war, and before the Uzice Corps came to town he went to Gorazde together with the head of the health centre across Cajnice and Pljevlja. He went on to his native birthplace Bijelo Polje and doctor -- the other doctor, the head of the centre, he went on to Tara, Dr. Uljarevic. He stayed there until the Uzice Corps came to town. At the initiative of the then war commander of the wartime hospital they managed to persuade his wife, also a doctor, medical doctor, and they even provided them with a driver to go and collect Dr. Safet and provide him with all the guarantees for his safety but that his services were needed in the town. They did so, managed to persuade him to come back to town. As he returned home an hour or two later, a group of armed individuals came and took him away. She told him that they manhandled him at the time, and unfortunately I must say that the doctor's body was identified at the Visoko cemetery. His remains were recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened to his house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Some two days after he had been taken away his house was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long had he returned to Visegrad before he was taken away by the men who ultimately killed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: According to the story of his wife, some three or four hours later. The same evening practically of his arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Up until now you've been describing to us events that occurred while the Uzice Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army was in Visegrad, ostensibly to safeguard and protect all Yugoslav citizens regardless of ethnicity. Do you remember what happened the day the Uzice Corps left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: When the Uzice Corps left I was woken one morning by fierce shooting in the town. The shooting could be heard from all the different quarters, and it came from sidearms. As I was on my way to work coming out of a side street onto the main street I saw a large column of military vehicles which indicated to me that the Uzice Corps was leaving the town of Visegrad. I went back home and informed my family about this. At my insistence and the insistence of my mother they left the town of Visegrad on the same day the Uzice Corps did. They took a bus at 10.00 in the direction of Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did your daughter go with your wife and your -- did your daughter travel with your wife out of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you Uzice Corps left Visegrad did the paramilitary groups leave as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Unfortunately, although we thought the paramilitaries left town too, that day at the meeting in the health centre, since the war command had gone, the new administrator remained working in the health centre, and he held a briefing, gathering all of us and told us that we need not be afraid for our safety, that a Territorial Defence was there for the town of Visegrad, and the Uzice Corps will return if necessary, but I believe he was trying a speech of appeasement or something. He was comforting us and he told us that the paramilitaries had left town as well, but unfortunately that wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After the Uzice Corps left town, did you have another incident with a group of armed men or -- in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I don't know which one you mean. There were several. Do you mean the incident in my apartment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us about the incident that occurred inside your apartment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. I initially thought you mean something else. There was an incident at my apartment. As I wasn't feeling quite safe at my home, I spent time at the house of my father-in-law, and one day I got a call from the owner of the building where I lived, who told me that unidentified persons had broken into my apartment. She doesn't know whether they had taken anything, but the door was broken in, and it would be a good idea for me to come to the apartment and shut the door somehow. I used byroads from Bikavac to reach my home, and while I was repairing the lock, a car stopped outside the house. Two soldiers came out armed. They asked, "Where is the key from the Mercedes in the garage?" I answered, "I really don't know. I just live here. You should perhaps ask upstairs," and at that moment the owner of the apartment building came with her daughter-in-law. They said they don't have the key, that their son, the owner of the Mercedes, had tried to leave town the day before, but in Dragobilje he and a large group of men were taken off the bus, and she doesn't have the keys, briefly. They left after leaving a piece of paper tacked on the garage door saying, "Occupied," with a signature Buco, B-u-c-o, and they came back with a man from a garage who tried to force open the door of the Mercedes and start it. All the while I was still there. I hadn't left yet. And the wife of the man who owned the house asked what happened to the men from that bus, and he said, "Dear lady, I really don't know if you had any family on that bus, but if you had, my condolences because none of them are alive." The woman started crying, of course. She broke down in a state of shock, and he said to me, "Would you come with me for a minute?" He took me into my apartment. We sat down at the dining-room table, and then he told me, "Do you want to buy your head?" I said, "What do you mean?" And he said, "Don't pretend you don't understand me. Give me all the valuables, the money, the hard currency, whatever you have; otherwise, I'll turn you over to the people -- to the men from Obrenovac and that's the end of you." I gave him the money I had, around 50 Deutschmarks, my wedding ring and that was it. Then we left my apartment again and went outside of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a specific question. When you were speaking the words "Turn you over to the guys from Obrenovac," you took your right index finger and you drew it across your neck. Is that what one of these men did, draw his finger across his neck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It's a gesture that means you will be killed. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it doesn't have to mean necessarily that I'll have my throat slit. It just means that's it with you, that you'll be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with a cherry red Passat that was readily recognisable in the Visegrad area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, very familiar. It's not exactly cherry red. It's dark, ripe cherry, burgundy red.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you know who owned that car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, I know the owner of the vehicle was Behija Zukic and her husband Dzemo. They owned a grocery shop not far from me. I shopped very often there even on the day when Dzemo had bought that car I went to congratulate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you heard that Behija Zukic had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. I found out at the health centre from my colleagues. They told me that Behija Zukic had been brought in to the morgue. She was brought dead. They also told me that the man at the mortuary who saw her said that she was butchered, that she had practically half her head missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the day that you learnt that she was brought to the morgue, were you at the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you see that car on the day that she was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty whether it was on the same day or the day after, but I saw the car. I'm quite sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances under which you saw the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It was around 10.00. Usually at the health centre breakfast is from 9.30 to 10.00, and the breakfast was usually served in the administration building. After that breakfast, I was meeting up with some friends because we usually had 10 or 15 minutes off after breakfast, and we met up in the secretary's office. From that office you have a good view of the entrance, the emergency entrance, and the parking lot outside the health centre. At one point that vehicle we're talking about drove in, and when you know who the owner of the vehicle is and that she's lying in the mortuary of the health centre, you become very curious to know who's driving the car now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you see who was driving the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It was a soldier in a camouflage uniform wearing trainers. I had seen the man a few times before, and from what I knew it was Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you decided it was no longer safe to stay in your apartment and you left your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I realised it was not safe to stay at my apartment, and I decided to move to the house where my wife was born to live with my father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And after you moved to that location did you still go to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I continued to go to work. But the reason I moved from my apartment was that in order to go to work from my apartment, I had to go through the entire high street and meet a lot of people, whereas from Bikavac I just had to cross a small bridge and I was already quite close to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you decided that you could no longer safely go to your workplace?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened that made you decide you could no longer safely go back and forth from work?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue. Can I ask you, though, this man you were referring to, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Thank you. He was a Serb, but we knew each other well. We often played billiards together, and he said, "What on earth are you doing here, man?" I said, "I'm going home from work." And he says, "You must be insane. If these men from Obrenovac catch you it's the end of you. You're done in." And I said, "What should I do?" And he says, "Go into hiding. I don't know. Do something. Go wherever you like, but don't stay here." And from then on I was in a daze. I hardly found my way home. And they saw the state I was in, so they escorted me almost all the way to the house where I was living then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you tried to leave Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. I tried twice. Once I tried to leave, and the second time I made an attempt it was under very special circumstances, but if you want to hear about my first attempt, I had --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention -- was there a time that when you tried to leave, you were turned back at a check-point when you tried to leave the town or tried to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why were you turned back at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was just going to say that. I had decided to risk everything and leave town after that warning I had received, and the only way was to take the bus, risk everything, go to the bus terminal and take the bus, and that's what I did. And whatever happens, at least I'll know that I have tried. We reached the check-point in Dobrun. When the bus was stopped, of course they wanted to see IDs and permits to leave town. Since at that time I did not have a permit to leave town, I was told that I couldn't go on, that I had to go back. They simply took me off the bus and said, "Be on your way." So they left me on the road 26 kilometres away from town, and they told me to go back. The only way to go back was to walk. And after half a kilometre, a kilometre, perhaps, a car passed by. I sort of hailed it by raising my arm. It was a very nice lady at the wheel, and she gave me a lift to Visegrad, for which I'm eternally grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At Visegrad were you told where you needed to go to try to obtain a permit to leave the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: They told me, "You don't have the permit." I said, "No. Where should I get one?" And they had said at the check-point, "You get it from a police station. Unless you do so, we can't let you through." They were rather polite and everything at the check-point, but they said, "Unfortunately, you will have to go back."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you go to the police station in Visegrad town and try to obtain a permit to leave the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. Since that lady who gave me a lift back to town lived close to my father-in-law's apartment, and that is close to the police station, I thought While I'm here, let me try. I went to the police station, and outside the police station there was a crowd, mainly women and children, and it was practically impossible to get to the door. Everybody was standing there and waiting. So I joined that crowd, started waiting, not knowing exactly what I was waiting for, and at one point one employee of the police station, a very good friend of mine, came by and said, "What are you doing here?" And I said, "I came here to get a certificate, a permit to leave town." And then he ushered me into the station. I stayed there perhaps half an hour. He arranged it all for me. He had to take the paper to the commanding officer to sign. At any rate, I got this certificate allowing me to leave the town issued by the official police authorities. That friend saw me out of the police station, wished me luck and that's how I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would like to now draw your attention to the 7th of June, 1992, the date that's the subject of the indictment against one of the accused. Do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that day very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to describe what happen in the afternoon of that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: As I said, I was in hiding that last week. I stayed at my father-in-law's house, not going out, and there was a friend with me hiding as well. We were hiding in the basement of my father-in-law's house. It was a small basement, very dark, and in the back there was an old cupboard where they were keeping some old stuff, and we hid behind that cupboard. He would go in first because he was a larger man than I and I followed. On the 7th of June, I can't tell you the exact time but it was sometime in the afternoon, I heard a car stopping, and we got into the basement. The house overlooks an intersection -- or, rather, a fork in the road, one going left, one going right. That car stopped for a while and then went on right towards Ban Polje. I could see then that it was my own car. The two of us did not dare get out of the basement. We didn't know how long they -- he would stay. I don't know how long we were waiting for, but the car eventually came back. This time the engine was turned off. Then since the road went downhill he just let it slide and stopped at the same intervention. He got out of the car, and at that time an old woman was passing by. I have to note at this point that there were many refugees in Visegrad from surrounding villages, so I didn't know that woman. It was just an old woman. That man asked her about me and she said, "I have no idea." And I heard him saying, "He must be around here somewhere." And then he got into the car again and continued slowly by car. Since if I get out of the house I can see the rest of the street leading to Visegrad Hotel, and for a while I did indeed look at the car, where it was going. The car stopped at the next house in the row. They got out, banged at the garage door, then got back into the car again and went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Whose car was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I've said already it was my own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue what happened then after the men left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: At that moment, seeing that the car is receding in the distance, I sat at a little bench outside and lit a cigarette. My friend was still in the basement. He hadn't got out at all. If you mean how long it all lasted, it was just a few minutes. My father-in-law was also there, and he said, "They're gone." And then he walked to the building, the structure nearby, his own outhouse, and I could see him walking for a while. He was keeping his hands behind his back. And at one moment he signed to me that I should get out of the way and hide. I did so because I couldn't see what he was seeing. And to get back into the basement I had to go through that opening, and as I was trying to cross to the basement I saw that from the direction of Mejdan four men in a row, side by side, that is, with just a couple of metres between them, were walking towards us, and I decided not to go into the basement because if they had seen me, my friend in the basement still has a chance of remaining undetected, and then, I don't know why, my friend also got out of the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, if I could stop you there, and if I can ask briefly to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, you were just beginning to describe what happened when your friend came out of the basement. Could you please continue to tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: As I said, I saw these four persons coming towards us. One of them passed us by, got into the basement. Not the basement where we were hiding but the basement of the entire house. It was also like an underground apartment. Another one stopped and stood by us. The third one did not even approach all the way but stood -- stopped and stood a few metres away, and the fourth one whom I had seen at the health centre passed by us and went upstairs. I don't know exactly how much time elapsed, perhaps a few minutes before they all came back, the one from upstairs and the one from the basement, and then we were three standing outside the house. And the person I mentioned today, Milan Lukic, was the one who had gone upstairs, and when he came back down it was obvious that they were waiting all for him. When he came down, he asked for our IDs. Inserted into my ID was the permit to leave town that I had obtained, and he looked at me and said, "Why are you hiding?" I said, "I'm not hiding. You found me here, so that means I'm not hiding." He looked at my permit to leave town, and he tore it into shreds, threw it on the ground and stepped on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the time that you're having this conversation with the person you're identifying as Milan Lukic, are you facing him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, face-to-face. We stood face-to-face.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I know you said this is in the afternoon, but can you describe what the leading conditions was -- were that day? Was there adequate light for you to see his face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. It was not late in the afternoon, it was early. It was before 5.00 p.m. at the very least, and it was summertime, and it was very light.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you please describe what he looked like to you at that stage? What was he wearing? What did his face appear to -- what did his face look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform but not the uniform I saw him in several days earlier. This time he wore the sort of camouflage uniform normally worn by the police, which is the purple-blue camouflage uniform. He had a beret on his head bearing the symbol of the -- of a two-headed eagle, and on every sleeve -- on both sleeve he had the two-headed eagle symbol, and on one of the sleeves there was written "Police." His face was also painted over the way you normally see faces painted in movies on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, while you were describing that to us, you were with both of your hands rubbing your hands from your cheek just next to your nose back towards are ears. Is that the portion of his face that was painted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. This area on both cheeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What else do you remember about his appearance that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I remember him wearing tennis shoes. Since I worked at the health centre, and this is something you asked me earlier about, one of the things that struck me at the time was a small Band-Aid that he had here on his arm. Rather, it was a small bundle of gauze covered by a Band-Aid, and this is something that I observed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you were describing that, the gauze, you were pointing to the inside of your right elbow. Is that the position where you remember seeing this piece of gauze?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. That's the spot where he had the gauze.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Based on your -- your medical training, under what circumstances would someone have a piece of gauze with a Band-Aid covering it? What did that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's something I said earlier. When I first saw the Band-Aid I thought that perhaps the person was under the influence of drugs. Normally you'd wear such type of bandage if you'd been injected with something or if you received intravenous infusion, blood drip, that's the sort of Band-Aid you'd have as a patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have any impression about whether he was intoxicated or whether his state of mind was altered in any way at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I was not able to observe him being under the influence of drugs or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the time he was having this -- this conversation with you, was he looking at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: We were looking at each other closely. Still today, as I recall that particular incident, I see that face before me. I don't think that there's an individual or a human being in the world who spends as much time with a person who wishes to kill him without remembering the face and the contours. That's something one cannot ever forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you remember if he was carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Let me just say that all the soldiers who came on that day were armed with automatic weapons, whereas Milan had a sniper rifle with a silencer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened after he had the conversation with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: After the conversation he said that we should follow him. We set out uphill toward a hill called Grad. I mentioned the intersection a moment ago, and we turned right on the intersection toward the Grad hill. He went first. I followed him. Then my friend followed me, and there was another man behind him carrying a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Some 200 metres into the town we stopped on the road. He motioned to us to stop. He entered a gate into the yard and then entered the house, searched the ground floor, came out and said, "Let's move on." Let me just say that the other soldiers who were there were no more than eight to ten in my assessment. So there were only eight to ten of them there. The other soldiers stayed back to search the houses. We proceeded toward Megdan across a meadow which lay to the right of the house where we stopped. As we walked in the meadow, somewhere halfway into the meadow, let me just say that between the Grad hill and Milavici there was a Territorial Defence check-point there, and this was the precise route that they took every day to reach the check-point, they went past that house. This was the regular Territorial Defence of Visegrad or the Serbian army. That's where they would normally pass by. And we heard shots from up there. Not that they were shooting at us necessarily. But we were told to stop again, and they shouted back, "Stop shooting at us." Then we continued walking. We stopped 500 metres later outside a house. We were told to stop there. He entered the house, searched all the rooms, upstairs too, and as he got out he told us that we should get into that very house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, when you say "he," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I'm referring to Milan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: He told us to get into the house. I remember well that the house had a large hallway from where there was a staircase to the upstairs room, and from that hallway one got into a very large living-room. There was an elderly man in the house whose name I don't know. He was either staying in the house or he was the owner. Milan went away leaving one soldier behind outside the door. That was the same soldier who accompanied us all the way to that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did there come -- you say he went away, Milan went away. Did there come a time when he came back to that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: While we were in the hallway I sat on the steps leading upstairs. I was quite crestfallen, if anybody's interested in knowing how I felt at the time. Well, it's the same as when a doctor tells you that you are terminally ill. You feel completely despondent. I was thinking along the line of, My God, what have I done? Have I done something bad in my leave to deserve this? I had never caused anyone to bear a grudge against me, let alone anything worse than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: The soldier who was in the doorway was, I must admit, very polite. He even chatted with my friend while we were there together with that old man. He asked him if he had any children. He said, "I do, two, two children, two sons." He said, "Well, why have you waited for so long? Why didn't you hide away somewhere safely?" He replied, "I don't know. Can I talk to Branimir Savovic?" He said, "I don't know. I can't tell you anything before I ask anyone."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who is Branimir Savic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Branimir Savovic was a very good friend of my friend. They were on visiting terms. He had a position at the time. He had been the president of the SDS while at the time I think he was the wartime president of the Visegrad municipality. Let me repeat that they were very close friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when this soldier relayed your friend's request to Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, a bit later. If you'll allow me, when I come to that point I'll tell the story. After a certain while, I really don't know how much time had elapsed -- I told you that time meant nothing to me at that point. That was one of the things that was least on my mind, to keep track of time. At a certain point Hasan Mutapcic entered the house with his son, a boy aged 13, I guess. He was wearing blue shorts and a black T-shirt. The child was scared out of his wits, trembling all over. I don't who accompanied Hasan Mutapcic to the entrance to the house because from where I was sitting I was only able to see the door and the soldier at the door, so I can't tell you who brought them over. At -- shortly afterwards, another individual was brought over to the house, another one, and then two of them. There were between 10 to 13 of us in the house at that point. I wasn't really keeping track of how many there were. Among those who arrived, there was Meho Dzafic and Ekrem Dzafic, father and son. I didn't know them well, but they were practically known to everyone in the town, both of them. Sometime later Milan returned, ordered us to stand in a semicircle in that room, to place all our valuables in the centre of the room, to take our shoes and socks off. He said, "If I find anything on anyone, I will kill them." We did as he asked. We placed all those things on the ground, and then he squatted down, took wallets one by one and taking banknotes out. As he took my wallet into his hands he found several names and telephone numbers there. He asked me, "Who are these individuals," and I said, "These are my family members from Sarajevo." Everyone, I guess, keeps a lucky charm with him. I had a dollar that I kept in my wallet. I kept it there as a lucky charm. You might call it superstition, but that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Groome, I see that you have estimated two and a half hours for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness is employing the narrative mode of telling his -- his tale, and I can understand that, but I believe we would proceed faster if you were to ask the witness particular questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The narrative approach, I think, can be modified --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- to advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can ask you a few questions about what's happening at this point. You spoke about Milan Lukic finding what your -- your good luck charm, a lucky dollar. After all the people put their belongings in front of him, what he do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: He scooped up all the money and said, "You said you didn't have any foreign currency, but I see you do." He said that scornfully. He put the money into his pocket and asked whose car was the Yugo parked behind the car. Meho said that this was his son Osman's car. He then asked him for the keys.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened to the identification papers belonging to all the men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: He kicked all the identification papers with his foot behind the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I draw your attention to -- was there a point in time when a soldier asked Milan Lukic about -- or conveyed the request of your friend regarding Branimir Savovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. I said that Milan Lukic went out with Meho Dzafic to get the keys to the car. When he returned, in the doorway leading to that room he was asked by the soldier who was standing in the doorway, "Milan, this man would like to talk to Branimir Savovic." His response was very rude or very impolite. He said, "Fuck his mother." He just waved this way, indicating my -- pointing to my friend. "You, you, you. All of you get out." We obeyed. And when I was saying you, you, you, I meant the four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to name the four people that Milan Lukic pointed to and said get out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That was Ekrem Dzafic, Hasan Mutapcic, I and my friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where did you go when you left the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: We got out of the house, and in the direction of the Bikavac Hotel there was a parked Yugo, that was Dzafic's son's car, and then ahead of that car there was the Passat vehicle parked, the one that we referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the colour of the Yugo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yugo was olive green. That's how we referred to that colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you approach the two cars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. We reached the car, and then he asked who had the driver's licence, and I answered I do. I wanted to sit at the wheel, but he said no, no, you. Then Ekrem said, "I have a licence." He seemed quite excited but was allowed to sit at the wheel. I sat in the back behind the driver's seat. Let me just note that Yugo has only two doors. That's how you get into the back. Next to me Meho Dzafic was sitting. They told us to move over a bit to make space and he was practically sitting in my lap. He was of quite large build, and Yugo is a small vehicle. Seated next to us was the same soldier who was with us all along and who remained standing outside the house. He sat in the back with us, and my friend sat next to the driver in the front seat, and the two other persons that I didn't know at the time, and Hasan Mutapcic, sat in the Passat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it the Chamber's intention to break at 10.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's a brief matter I would like to address the Chamber on. Would it be convenient to excuse the witness now and I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you are excused. You will return at 20 minutes after 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, a few weeks ago the Prosecution filed a motion to add an exhibit to our list in our rebuttal or -- and to rebut the evidence of Milan Lukic. It's a protocol book from the Visegrad medical centre. Mr. Alarid has responded, I think in the last few days. It occurred to me yesterday, as we have someone here from the Visegrad medical centre, I showed him a photocopy of that book, and he's able to authenticate the book and to -- and to interpret how the book is used and the columns on it. It seems to me to be prudent to raise this with the Chamber if it were possible for the Chamber at some time before the end of his testimony to consider the matter and issue an oral decision. I would seek to have this witness address the book at this stage rather than trying to find an additional witness who could authenticate the book later on in the trial. I think it would save considerable time and expense, so I would ask if the Court be able to possibly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would be eminently sensible. We will do that. Well, Mr. Groome, I wanted to say though that you have to move more quickly with this witness. At this rate you will probably take more than the two and a half hours, and then there's the cross-examination by the two counsel. We are falling behind, and I am considering measures to be adopted to compensate for any time that might be lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I take it under consideration. I do try to -- I am conscious of the time. Sometimes it's -- with these witnesses it is difficult to find places to cut their evidence. I have cut a considerable amount of his evidence already, but I will endeavour to take him more briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And the same thing applies to Defence counsel. We have to proceed expeditiously, and at the same time fairly. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll give the decision in relation to the Prosecution's motion filed on the -- we need to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, in the interest of time Mr. Alarid informs me that he will be introducing your statement or seeking to introduce your statement into evidence, so many of the details of what happened prior to the arrival at the river will be well known to the Chamber. I'd like to get to what happened at the river as expeditiously at possible, but there are some questions that I do need to ask you, so could I ask you -- could you give me precise answers to -- to a few questions and then I'll let you explain in detail what occurred when you arrived at the riverside. The first question I want to ask you is when you left the Bikavac area, where did you go? Where did you travel to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: We travelled to the hotel Vilina Vlas in Visegradska Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the trip to the Vilina Vlas hotel did you pass by the location of the two mosques in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court what you observed about the two mosques?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: When you go down from Bikavac towards the centre of town, on the left-hand side the first mosque is the old Visegrad mosque. I saw that it had burnt down. It had been torched. And as we continued towards Vilina Vlas hotel, crossing over the Rzava bridge, I saw that the other mosque had also been torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the Vilina Vlas hotel did it appear that it was open for business?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It was not. There was not a single indication that the hotel was operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the registrar to publish from our Sanction system, I have put the 360 -- what we refer to as the 360 programme up. Do you recognise the image that is now visible on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. That's the entrance into the Vilina Vlas hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can ask Mr. Van Hooydonk to bring us into the lobby. VG-32, I'm going to ask Mr. Van Hooydonk just to pan around the lobby. I'd ask you not to comment, but then I'll ask you to comment on specific places that I'll ask him to then stop at. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could I ask you to go back, pan a little left. Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What area are we looking at here, VG-32?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That part of the lobby where the reception desk is is where Mitar Vasiljevic was standing when we entered the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can see a person standing in this image. Is that person standing at the reception desk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask -- I'm sorry. Please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: We were standing there, except we were facing the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You were standing against that reception desk facing outward from it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, facing the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I'd ask us to pan around a bit more and stop there. What is that to the right of the reception area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It's the entrance to the dining area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we could pan right again. Stop there. What are we looking at here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I think it's the elevator and the staircase going up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we could pan again, please, to the right. Please stop.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's the entrance to the hotel seen from the reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask the registrar to now call up 65 ter number 101.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And while that's being done, in preparation for your giving evidence in the Mitar Vasiljevic case, did you draw a diagram indicating where all of the main participants were during the time that you were all in the lobby of the Vilina Vlas hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked to draw from memory a sketch of the entrance to the hotel, a sketch of the reception area and designate the places where we were standing as well as the other persons who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: 65 ter 101 is now up on the screen. Are you able to see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that the diagram that you yourself drew about where people were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There are seven blank circles at the top part of the diagram. What do they indicate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: These seven circles are the seven of us, the seven persons standing, leaning on the reception desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The circle that has the initials ML in there, what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: As I said, Milan Lukic, who went behind the reception desk looking for keys, and the arrow leading right is the reception itself, and the one leading up is behind the reception desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the circles with the initials MV, what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's Mitar Vasiljevic, where he was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the empty circle directly across the lobby from Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That shows the person where the soldier was standing who trained his rifle at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long were you in the lobby of the Vilina Vlas hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I've said earlier that it's very hard for me to judge. It could have been five, ten minutes, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you able during this period to have a clear observation of Milan Lukic and his face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, because Milan Lukic came in together with us into the lobby of the hotel. I could clearly see that he went behind the reception desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you left the hotel where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: As I said, when we left the hotel we were ordered to go back in to the vehicles, to sit exactly as we were sitting before, and we drove on to Sase.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived in Sase?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: When we arrived at the intersection at Sase, we turned not towards Visegrad as we had expected but to the right towards Visegradska Zupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what happened when you turned right at Sase?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: When we turned to the right at Sase, we stopped about 500 metres on, close to a building that I believe was a warehouse owned by Purisa Markovic. I know that to the right of that building there were a couple of houses and this small settlement, this building and the few houses around was called the Jasarevic. That's where we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you stopped at that location, what happened? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: When we stopped there, the Passat vehicle was ahead. We were behind them, and they drove on from the intersection at Sase a bit faster, and as we caught up with them Mitar Vasiljevic, Lukic, and the person who was in the Passat all the time had already gotten out. We were ordered to get out too, and we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what happened next.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: As we got out of the car, the demeanour of the soldiers changed dramatically. In my earlier statement, I said that the soldier who was with us had been rather kind, but that all changed dramatically. We were ordered to walk towards the Drina River, which was to our left, to the left of the road. Some 100 metres by the Drina River was a meadow, and we walked across the meadow. And if there had been a trace of hope that this could all somehow have a happy ending, this trace of hope was extinguished as we walked through the meadow. We were walking not in a group but in a certain disposition. I was in the middle. To my left, if I remember correctly, was VG-14. To the far left was my friend, and at one point I tried to sort of lean to the left to come closer to him, because it was clear to me what was going to happen, but this attempt was thwarted very crudely. After a minute or two we reached the riverbank, the trees lining the riverside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened after you reached the trees at the riverbank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: When we got to the willow trees lining the river I saw that the water level was low and that from the water to the spot where we were standing on a small plateau there were about ten metres, like the length of this room -- or, rather, the width of this room. We stopped on a grassy spot, a couple of square metres. When we stopped, Milan asked, "Who can swim?" I really don't know why I said what I said, but I said that I can swim. I know that many of the others could swim too, but at that moment I knew very clearly what was going to happen, and I thought since I was forced to watch, I should go first in order not to see the rest. And he said, "Come on then." I started walking towards the water, and that moment, heard Meho saying, "For Christ's stake, Mitar, what are you doing?" And from my left I heard my friend pleading as well, "Come on, people. Don't kill us. What have we done to you?" But all this transpired in a haze as far as I'm concerned. After I made the first few steps I was half frozen. I was frozen, and I wanted those last ten metres -- I wanted to go those last ten metres with only my daughter in my mind. At that time, nothing else around me existed. I only thought of her playing in her room. I really don't know how long it took me to make those few steps to the very edge of the river, but at one point when I reached the edge I heard a voice saying, "Stop," and I stopped. Then they ordered the others to walk to the river and to line up next to me and they did. They started approaching. To my right was Ekrem. Next to him his father. To my left was Hasan Mutapcic. I believe next to him was VG-14, and after him a man I didn't know, and to the far left was my friend. And at that moment when we stopped, I heard a question, "How are we going to fire?" And I heard the answer, "Single shots." And then you heard the cocking of the rifle and the switching of the mechanism to single shots. On three different sides you heard that sound. At that moment, I got a glimmer of hope again. I thought that since four of them were going to fire single shots, maybe there is a puny chance that if I'm not hit by the first shot I could dive into the river and try to swim under water. That was my first thought. I have to say here that it's like a movie on fast forward. It's the survival instinct. Things move at the speed of lightning. And as I thought that, I heard Meho's scream that was not even uttered to the end. It was frozen midway. And I must say I didn't even hear the shot at that moment. As I jumped into the river and as I was falling into the water, there between the sand and the water I -- I saw clearly a red blood stain. Falling into the water I heard shots and screams, the screams of the others, and I must say they were not all fatally wounded by the first shot. I have to admit that around me there was chaos at that moment, inferno with hellfire that I cannot describe with mere words. It's not something you can describe unless you've lived through it. When my body hit the water, I realised I wouldn't be able to stay under, and I decided to make a little manoeuvre to turn around, because the water level was just one metre underneath the bank, and if I was under the water I couldn't see them, of course. I decided to turn back towards the bank, and you know the water creates a little sand bank. I put my head on it. Consciously or unconsciously I can't honestly say, I pushed my arms into the sand under me. I must have been doing that unconsciously. And since I had dug my head under into the sand at first, I realised I couldn't stay in that position long and at that moment I turned my head sideways by half so that my one eye and one side of the face were out of the sand, and at that moment I saw Hasan and that he was wounded and that he was trying to dig his way crawling into the bank and that the sand was falling over him as he was coming closer to me. And at that time I was wondering, does a dead man have his eyes open or closed? I decided, nevertheless, to close my eyes and let it be. I heard steps approaching. I heard a shot and the sound that was like somebody taking a body up in their arms and dropping it, dropping it right onto me. I felt the body falling on my neck and that body covering all of mine. The weight of that body dragged me under, under the water, but fortunately, as I said, my arms were dug deep into the sand and that provided me with enough purchase to stay aboveboard myself together with the body. To my other side Ekrem had fallen silent. There were no more sounds from him. There was another shot from the right, and then another on the far right approximately where my friend had been, and then silence fell, complete silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, did this come a time when the men who had done this left that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I have just a few words more to say and then it's the end. That man who had approached, I heard the shots and then I heard him saying, "Here's another one who is alive -- here's one who is alive," and I thought he meant me. I thought I was the only one who survived, and in those couple of minutes I saw again the vision of my daughter. However, did he not mean me. I heard another shot fired into a body in the water, and then the steps moved away. And a couple of minutes later I opened my eyes, and the view that opened before me was a young man looking around him, and that was VG-14. I asked him if he was wounded. He said no. He asked me the same. I said, "I'm not wounded either." He said, "What are we going to do now?" I said, "Wait till they're gone." And when we heard them driving away, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Mr. Groome, this story is of course very moving and that's why I haven't interrupted it, but you must know what evidence you need from the witness, and we both come from jurisdictions where frequently lawyers are told control your witness. So although the witness has a story to tell and there's a lot of emotion in it, you know what evidence you want to elicit. Don't allow him to run away with -- with the story, because your time will be up at 20 minutes after 11.00. You would have used two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour, and for the record all of what the witness has just said is evidence that we tend to rely on and I took the view that it was more expeditious rather than have me interrupt him with what happened next or precise questions. So I will be relying on all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, if I could ask you some follow-up questions. Did there come a time when you were able to determine how many detainees died there at the river's edge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Five. Quite simply, when I got out of the water the first thing I did was to see if anyone was alive. No one was. And when we crossed to the other side of the river, I spent there one week and I went every day to a hill to see that place again from the hill and all those days the bodies were still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So for five days after this happened, you were able to see the remains of the other men who were with you and were shot at the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness to this day remains in contact with the families of the other victims and has advised me that the graphic description of the injuries of those victims in public causes them great distress. I do not intend to ask any more detailed questions about those injuries to establish that those men died. I believe I have done that. He asked me should the Defence or the Chamber require more precise information that he be allowed to provide that private session. I'd like to now call up 65 ter number 102.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again VG-32, in preparation for your testimony in the Vasiljevic case did you prepare a diagram showing the location of you and the other people who were present at the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is the diagram we're now looking at 65 ter 102 a photograph of that diagram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do the initials ML and MV stand for respectively Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic as they did in the previous diagram that we've looked at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do the initials in the -- in the seven circles that are by the water, do they indicate the initials of the victims as best you know the position of the different people -- where the different people were at the time they were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, and just the way I've explained. The line and the order in which we stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At some point after this event did you go to the village of Medjedja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you were there were you asked by a former colleague, a doctor from the Visegrad medical centre, to establish a clinic in Medjedja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that so? Mr. Groome, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is correct, but we're not calling at that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I in error forgot to formally tender the diagram so could I at this stage tender 65 ter number 102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it. MR. GROOME.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: MR. GROOME: Did there come a time when you were --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Your Honours, 102 will become Prosecution Exhibit P65.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were asked to treat a young woman who it turned out you knew quite well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if necessary, use the pseudonym sheet in front of you, but can you identify this young woman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. That's VG-114. I have to say that we were very good and close friends with her, both I and my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe her condition as best you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It is very difficult to describe the state she was in when I saw her. I don't think such a scene can be presented in a single horror movie. Let me just tell you that this was an individual that I knew and that I could hardly recognise when I saw her. Her entire face was black, burnt. It was a wound. Both her arms were bandaged, but they were not medical bandages. Those were just makeshift bandages, five or six of them. The wounds were so infected that when I tried to change the bandages and dress her wounds on her, whilst one arm as I took a couple of layers of the bandages I saw maggots coming out. I fainted at the sight of it. I came to several minutes later and continued dressing her wound. That was the first time I dressed her wounds. Let me just say that the person --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry, please finish your sentence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Let me just say that that person had long hair before the war coming down to the small of her back. When I saw her on that occasion her hair was closely clipped and it was lice ridden, millions of lice. I didn't have any remedies --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: -- for that and we agreed that she should shave her head.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter number 174. It's a set of three pictures. I'd ask that this not be shown publicly but only to those of us in the courtroom and ask you do you recognise what is depicted in these three photographs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. That's the person, number 114. The black part of her face that you see, that's the way her entire face looked like. And the photograph was taken, you can judge how long after she had shaven her head, because you can see her hair has grown in the meantime. So the first time I saw her she shaved her head, and the photograph was taken at the time when her hair has grown thus long. So two to three weeks. You can see how her face was charred.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This particular photograph has an eight-digit number 4513 [Realtime transcript read in error "4153"] so the record is clear what photograph you're referring to. Could I ask that we advance to the next photograph in this series. This eight-digit number ends in 4514. Does that describe the condition of her as well as her hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I said that the photograph was not taken the first time I saw her, but this is the way both her arms looked like, and that's the way the other side of the arm that you can't see looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we please advance to the third photograph. This ends in 4515. And again is this another accurate depiction of how VG-114 appeared around the time that you were treating her for her burns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you present when a video was -- video interview was done of VG-114?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in fact were you present or attempting to treat her at the time they were filming the video and interviewing VG-114?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. The people making the footage wanted to film her wounds, and I had to take her bandages off for the film to be made. If that footage will be shown later on in the course of these proceedings and if in that footage I should appear, I would kindly request the Court to erase that bit, because the footage is quite long and the sequence where I'm shown can be taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just want to show one still from that video and if we switch to the Sanction system and I'm showing you a still from the video 65 ter 173.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is this the video that -- that you've been describing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. That's me. Can it please not be broadcast in the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We will not broadcast it in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender 65 ter number 174, the series of three photographs, as well as 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- 65 ter number 173, this video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 173 will become Exhibit P66 under seal and 65 ter number 174 will become exhibit P67 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask that the registrar show you a Defence exhibit from the Mitar Vasiljevic case. It's Defence Exhibit D26 and I asked the registrar yesterday to remove it from the registrar's vault and bring it to the courtroom for today. Could I ask you to take a look at D26. Could we please put it on the ELMO so the Chamber and the others in the court can see what the witness is looking at. While that's being done, can I ask you in the course of your work at the Visegrad medical centre was there a book that was used that was referred to as a protocol book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the function of a protocol book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: The protocol book was there to register all the patients coming to the clinic for treatment. So it's a register of patients or a daily protocol book or logbook of the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the book that's on the ELMO contains personal medical information of other people not connected with this trial, so could I ask that it not be broadcast, if it could be left on the ELMO so that we can see it but that it not be broadcast beyond this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to take a look at what's in front of you on the ELMO. Do you recognise what this book is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Normally the first column --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: -- stood for the name of the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
