utterances.text: Before I ask you to describe what's in there, could I ask you just whether you recognise the book that's in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know it very well, because we used the same sort of book even before the war. I will not go into great detail, but I can see that this book has almost been filled out, so there must have been hundreds of entries. So that's the one, the one that was used throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender what was D26 in the Mitar Vasiljevic case into evidence in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be admitted as P68 under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to find the entries for the 7th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Do you want me to find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. If you would look through and turn to the page where the people that were treated on the 7th of June begins. Have you found the page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: This is where the 7th of June starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to hand the witness a yellow sticky note. It's there, up there right on the desk. Could I ask you to please just mark that page so that when we do use this book we will be able to find this readily. Does this --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Do you mean where the page containing the entries for that day starts?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it correct that the people who were treated that day are listed in the order they were treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That was the customary practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do the entries for the 7th of June continue on the next two pages? Can I --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- ask you to turn to the next page and place a note on that page? When I asked you to look at a photocopy of this book yesterday, did you see the name of Milan Lukic for the 7th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to point to it with your finger so that the Chamber can see the entry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does it record his date of birth or his year of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The initials TO that we see in the second from the -- column from the right, what does that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Normally while I worked there we used this to denote Territorial Defence, whoever was in some way connected with the army or police and didn't have on them the health care booklet with their health insurance number were normally enter into the book as TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we move to the right-hand section of the entry and does it record what treatment he received on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Since a diagnosis would normally be entered on the other page, which would be written into the book by the doctor himself or herself, the next column would say what the doctor's prescription was. I can see here that we have 50 per cent glucoses, licocene [phoen] and baramisine [phoen]. That's as far as I'm able to make out the handwriting, and then lastly there would be a note or a remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does it say how the medicine was administered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's what I was about to say. The last column which says "Remark" is where the doctor would normally state the way in which the medication is supposed to be administered. I see that here it says intra-muscular and intravenous, which means that this was the way that the glucoses and the other medication was supposed to be administered depending on what the prescription of the doctor was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, I just have three more questions for you. What time did this shift start? What time of the day were patients first seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the 7th of June was a Sunday. If it was a Sunday, the shift started at 7.00 in the morning and lasted for 24 hours. That was the regimen at the time I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate the approximate amount of time that each patient would take in a doctor's visit at the centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Calls for speculation. Also, this witness was not present in the hospital or ordinarily worked there on this date in question and I believe it would be an improper opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I agree with you, because he works in the field. He works at the hospital. Are you in a position to answer that question, Witness, and tell us the basis of your knowledge? Are you in a position to estimate the amount of time a patient would take in a doctor's visit at the centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, any of these patients when they come to see a doctor, they don't go there merely to tell the doctor that they want to be prescribed with such-and-such a medication. I don't think that there's a single doctor who operates this way. First there is an exchange of greetings, then the doctor hears the problems that the patient has, then the data has to be entered into the appropriate documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just give us -- can you just give us an estimate of the time? This is what we want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 15 and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My last question is how many patients were treated before Milan Lukic was treated that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: We can count them all up. One, two, three, four, five, six , seven, eight, nine, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 -- so he was the 15th patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. In addition to -- because this has confidential medical information I believe it's appropriate that it be kept under seal. I've asked Mr. Van Hooydonk to prepare a photo of the two pages that are in question, but he has redacted the names of all the other patients. I'd ask that -- I'd seek to tender that at this time as a public exhibit so that we do not compromise the confidential medical information of the other people who went to the hospital at that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let that be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do I need to wait for a number to be assigned or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Are you clear, court, deputy, as to what you are to do?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Hasn't the number been assigned already for the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a matter that we can clarify after the break. And that concludes the questions that I have for you, VG-32. Thank you very much. Your Honour, I neglected to formally introduce 65 ter 101. I believe I have laid the foundation for it. I'd asked that it be admitted at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 101 will become Exhibit number P69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good morning, VG-32.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: My name is Jason Alarid and I'm the attorney for Milan Lukic. I'd like to ask you some questions about your testimony today and possibly earlier statements. Do I have your permission to ask you questions? And you nodded in the affirmative, but of course the recording and the court reporter cannot normally catch that, so we do need to have an answer loudly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: All right. And let's talk about first, just so we can get this over with, the logbook that you just looked at. Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you counted 14 entries before the entry with the name Milan Lukic; correct? And would it be fair to say that there was about nine entries after that? Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. Well, no. I apologise. I didn't count the patients following Milan. If you remember, I only counted the patients up to number 15 but not onwards. Perhaps we can count them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And let's do that, please, briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Nine. Yes, exactly nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And looking at the nine entries afterwards, so we can say that in the 24-hour period of that day 23 people were seen. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's what it seems, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. But you indicated that the shift on Sunday would start at 7.00 a.m., but in fact wouldn't it be fair to say that during the war the hospital would have been open 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the shift -- or let me explain this to you in simple terms. If you take over the shift at 7.00 in the morning and you're on duty for the next 24 hours, you hand over your shift to someone else on the following morning at 7.00 in the morning. So the shift working from 7.00 in the morning on Saturday worked until Sunday 7.00 in the morning when they were taken over by another stint that lasted until Monday 7.00 a.m. I said that this is the way they worked while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, sir, that makes sense to me, and so would it be fair that actually the person from the day before wrote the date where -- and you would write that date in at midnight when the 7th occurred; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That would be logical the way you put it. However, the practice employed at the Visegrad health centre at the time was such that the new shift arrived in the morning and that's when they would start working. I don't -- they might have written the entry at midnight, but I don't think so. This would normally be done at 7.00 in the morning when the new shift arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So are you saying that someone that was seen, let's say hypothetically at 2.00 a.m. in the morning, they would be actually listed on the day before? That doesn't sound logical.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It's not logical, but it can happen. But if you really want me to tell you the truth, while I was working, from midnight until the morning doctors were usually asleep unless we had an emergency, a real emergency. In that case the doctor would be called up and he would examine the patient. That was allowed, of course. They were not doing anything wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And for simple things like a glucose injection, might it be just a tech that handles that patient or a nurse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: They cannot write prescriptions. If I said -- I read the code of the diagnosis. Only the doctor can do that. Only he is qualified. And in addition you see the stamp of the doctor, which means the doctor was working that day. That's how you can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in terms of the doctor was there just one doctor on duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Usually only one doctor was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, if -- if the date wasn't being meticulously changed at the midnight hour, that makes it possible that an entry actually occurred on the next day, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, if -- if the new shift started at 7.00 a.m. and the first person at 7.00 a.m. put the date June 7th, then it's possible that patients ahead of that that were seen on June 7th are listed on the previous day, and if that was done on successive days that means patients could be listed on the wrong day if they showed up between midnight and 7.00 a.m. in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No. If they were examined between midnight and 7.00 as you are suggesting, it's the team that saw him that made the entry. It couldn't happen that somebody was seen and writes a new date in the morning and says, "Oh, we have already seen three patients. Let's post-date them." The entry would be -- of the date would be made at midnight or at 7.00. I'm telling you what the practice was. The rest is all theory. I'm telling you what the practice was and how the entries were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When the reality, of course, is you weren't there on the date to monitor the entries or see the flow of patients on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so it's possible that the entries are incorrect unless you, of course, could have verified that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Correct. How could I verify that if I told you I wasn't there? Finally, I was only asked to comment on this list. I saw it, and I told you what I had to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in the area of Visegrad and in Bosnia and Serbia is Milan a common name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: You could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is Lukic a common surname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: You could say so too. It's still common.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is Milan Lukic a common name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: You could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in being able to comment on the practice of the hospital, why aren't specific birth dates or better identification measures taken of patients seen at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Usually the year of birth was entered in this first column, but if you have a medicare card you would enter the number of the medicare card and the unique personal number. And I told you that wherever you see TO, that indicated soldiers or Territorial Defence members who did not have proper medical IDs so we just wrote TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I note in the entries there, some patients where no information is given, neither medicare or medicard information nor the date of birth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's something you have to ask the people who made these entries. I really don't know anything about it. I've said so before. They probably didn't do their job properly, or they had no access to the IDs or medicards. For instance, if a man aged 50 comes off the street, has no medicard and is not a member of the Territorial Defence and says, "Doctor, I have a problem," do you think the doctor would turn him away just because he doesn't have health insurance cards? That never happened. His personal details would be entered from his words but the patients were always admitted. Nobody was ever turned away that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, can you recognise the doctor's handwriting, or could this be a nurse entry or some other support staff entries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Very unlikely. The diagnosis and the method of administration or therapy were always entered by the doctor. But from this distance I really can't judge if it was a nurse or a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So could two separate people be making entries on the same book or more than one person making entries, i.e., a support staff takes initial check-in information and then a doctor writes in the diagnoses and the treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That could happen too. The nurse could write down the name and the doctor would write the diagnosis and the therapy. I told you already I cannot say more if I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is it possible that people that would come in and give a different name, especially during war times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Well, now we have strayed into the area of pure theory, possible versus impossible. I really can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And were there any Muslim doctors working shifts at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Do you mean at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I don't think so. I wasn't there the last week. I've told you I didn't work the last week. I've mentioned this before, and I don't know whether any Muslims were still working there. Maybe dentists, but I really don't think so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serbian doctors were available to treat patients at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Well, there were a couple of Serb doctors, even some who had gone to Uzice before the war to work there were made to come back. I know of some, but again I have to repeat I don't know how many doctors were on staff at that particular time and how many of them were Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But otherwise before the chaos started, it was a mixed hospital with staffers of both ethnicities working together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, moving kind of backwards in terms of your dealings with VG-114, did you -- did she tell you how she was burned, like with oil or gas or explosive device?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, she told me how she was burned. She told me that a tragedy had happened to her, that in a house -- I don't know exactly how many people she said. I really doesn't know the number, but a lot of people were set on fire in that house. Her mother and sister and one of her sister's two children. You have to realise the state she was in, and in view of the state she was in I had no right, moral or otherwise, to ask her to tell the story. It's just that occasionally in our conversations some of that would come up now and again, but I really couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did she tell you who helped this young lady in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. She was helped by a Muslim woman who lived in that town at that time, and she also said that a doctor had come from the health centre together with a nurse to examine her. And even on one occasion she told me that she had gone to a check-point once to ask the soldiers there to kill her because she couldn't go on living in that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, she was put on video after that time, but did you also give a statement to a TV show regarding the ordeal at the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It was not a TV show. It could have been a video film.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you remember describing the incidents on the Drina to that journalist or whatever it was, video recording?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, I described it. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you mention that there was a soldier from across the river that disrupted this execution by shooting and causing the Chetniks to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: You are labouring under a delusion. It's not me. The person who mentioned there was shooting from the other side of the street is not related to this incident. I know who you're talking about. It concerns two brothers who swam across the river. I never said anything like that. I say with full responsibility before this Court that I had never ever stated that somebody had shot from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who was the person that -- that made the statement about someone shooting from the other side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I can give a written statement about that if you wish. I don't want to say in public who this person is, and I don't know whether this person will appear before this Tribunal at all. I can give the Prosecution a written statement identifying that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, can we have P56, please, on the screen for the witness as reference.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Are we in private session? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: We have shown this before in private session. If I remember correctly, Your Honour, this document was discussed in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not being broadcast. It's not being broadcast, so it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I just want to know whether we are in private or open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're in open session, public session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Prosecutor showed this document on the screen, we discussed it then in private session, because that's what the Prosecutor asked. At least that's my memory. I would prefer it not to have this document broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us go to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just want to make some quick corrections to the record. With respect to Prosecution Exhibit 67, that's a series of three photographs, the record records me as referring to the first photograph as 4153. In fact it's an eight-digit number ending in 4513. With respect to the second photograph, the record records me as saying 4614. It is an eight-digit number ending with 4514, and finally the last photograph I'm recorded as saying 4615. I'd ask that the record identify that third photograph as an eight-digit number ending in 4515. With respect to Prosecution Exhibit number 68, that was the large book. In consultations with the registrar, because only two pages are necessary, to avoid scanning the many hundreds of pages that are included in that book, may I make the following suggestion to the Chamber: That the original physical copy be returned to the Vasiljevic file as D26 and kept there so that if there's ever a forensic examination required the book can be retrieved and we know the chain of custody and that P68 now be replaced with images of the two relevant pages containing information about the 7th of June, 1992, and that document be unredacted and remain under seal. Prosecution Exhibit 70 is a redacted version of the same two pages and is currently a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to add something related to Exhibit number P68, the book from the hospital of Visegrad, Visegrad hospital. My learned friend Mr. Groome requested just two pages. I would like to request some additional pages, actually just two more pages related to 14th of June, 1992, under the number 5353 and related to Mitar Vasiljevic, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would request from a chain of custody perspective and also for the benefit of the Court that the document, the book itself be transferred to the file of Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic in its entirety, namely because one, the Vasiljevic case is over. So there's no need for it to be part of the record there in terms of an appeal or something like that. And with regards to this, we -- considering the Court's earlier ruling of the 400 and some-odd pages of individual PDFs, by the time we get to look at in its entirety, there may be other relevant arguments relating to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take time to consider the various submissions and give a ruling later. Let us proceed with the case, with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. 32, we were looking at your diagram, and you indicated that you did not look behind you to see the exact location of the shooters, but this was more representative of where everyone was in the procession across the field that was 1 to 200 metres. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, is it true that -- that you walked across the field with people to both the left and the right of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. I said exactly the other time and today that as I was heading across the field, to my left was Witness 014. You can see on the diagram here that that witness is not on my left. Let me repeat. I was asked to draw these -- the disposition of the four circles was as it was at the time that I started walking toward the riverside. I didn't turn back and can't tell you what the disposition was at the time as I was heading towards the river. That's something that I said and I stand by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you did not walk across the field in a column but more in a row.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in terms of the description of each of the these people, you described Milan Lukic as wearing blue camouflage and a beret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What colour of beret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Blue. Light blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So similar to the colour of, let's say, the curtains behind Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: One could say so. Perhaps a bit darker.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how was Mitar Vasiljevic dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic had the Territorial Defence uniform which I described as olive-grey. It wasn't a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: And had a black hat on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the black hat, was it -- what kind of hat was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Well, what type was it. It was larger hat, not your classic western hat, but it had a larger rim. It was a typical American hat. I'm really not adept at describing hats. You can have millions of sorts. I can only draw it perhaps. I don't know how to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the colour of the hat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The -- black. Okay. And the other two gentlemen, the other two soldiers, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: They had ordinary camouflage uniforms. In other words, they were not police camouflage uniforms, they were regular camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Anything on their heads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I think that the soldier that I mentioned who was at Visegrad Banja didn't have anything on his head. I remember that well. Whereas the other soldier wore a beret, I think, but I can't be sure. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you remember the colour? Whether it was a beret or not, can you remember the colour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really cannot remember at this time what the colour of the beret was. You have to keep in mind the situation I was in. At that point that -- the colour of the beret was a thing of least concern to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could you recall whether the blue camouflage uniform was a short sleeve or a long sleeve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I think it was a short-sleeved one. I think I said so already. Are you referring to the police uniform? Are you referring to the police camouflage uniform or the soldier's camouflage? The police one was short sleeved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you notice any tattoos on the arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in terms of the face of the person that you say is Milan Lukic, you indicated that there was -- that only the cheeks were black, or was it the nose, the chin, and the forehead as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I said that he was painted like this. This part of his face was painted. There may have been some paint on the forehead as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you notice any pronounced mole on the face of this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that the first time that you saw Milan Lukic was with other soldiers in a cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And before that date you did not know Milan Lukic or anyone that could be named Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so even though you had been a long-time resident of Visegrad, you had not had any opportunity to come into contact with the local Milan Lukic or anyone else named by Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And even that time in the cafe, you didn't know the gentleman's name. It was only other people that told you what his name was. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And on what occasion would there be for someone to tell you who that was? Can you tell me the context of that identification?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I said that I saw him for the first time at the entrance to the cafe that we called Kod Pipe near the entrance to Panos. I said that he carried a rifle with a silencer. He struck me as someone who stood out, and I was interested in who he was. I was told that he was Milan Lukic, though I must say I didn't pay that much attention to this. When I saw this individual later, I noticed that it was him, that that same person was outside the health centre and later with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So it was only through someone else telling you it was Milan Lukic that you made the connection but not by any personal knowledge over time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And even then you said even though you say that that person stood out, there was nothing to distinguish him as a White Eagle or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: But likewise there was nothing to indicate that he was a member of the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was he wearing in the cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: He had regular camouflage uniform at the time. The same one that he had when I saw him once more later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this would be a green camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And are you saying he had a sniper rifle in the cafe or the next time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That time too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You did not indicate that in your first statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, yes, at that time in the cafe. That's something that caught my eye. Otherwise I would not have paid as much attention to him. There weren't many soldiers who carried a sniper rifle with a silencer around at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But there were other soldiers that carried sniper rifles with silencers on them, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Well, there probably were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you never got very close to him in that cafe, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at the cafe you didn't have any indication from the person of where this Milan Lukic was from or who his parents were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what date was this chance meeting at the cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I really don't know what date it was. I said that I had seen him before and that was at the time when the Uzice Corps was still there. I got back on the 25th or 26th, so it could have been in that period up until the 19th of May. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you can't place it at the beginning of your return to the Uzice Corps, [indiscernible] it could at any time in those three weeks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the time at the hospital, what was the date Behija Zukic was brought into the morgue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I think it was a day or two after the departure of the Uzice Corps. I'm not certain of the date though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And are you certain that this was the day that Behija Zukic was killed, or it could have been sometimes after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I really don't know whether it was on the same evening or on the same day, but I don't think that somebody would bring the body over to the morgue three or four days later. I really don't know how long it might take for someone to bring a body to the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you don't have a sense of how long it had been since Ms. Zukic had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I don't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you were identified in the cafe -- or excuse me, Milan Lukic was identified in the cafe, who told you who it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Well, I was with a couple of my acquaintances at the time. I can't really tell you that it was Mr. So-and-so who told me that that was Milan Lukic. This was not a big town. I said that it was acquaintances who told me so, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you say Ms. Zukic was brought into the morgue, do you recall who delivered the body to the morgue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I said that I was not present, and I don't remember. I don't recall ever stating who was it who brought the body over. I only said that the body was brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's why I was asking you if you knew. Now, you indicate that when Milan -- the person that you knew to be Milan Lukic came in a VW Passat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you indicated in your statement to the OTP that you believed that he had taken this Passat after allegedly killing her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I didn't say that I believed so. I said that I had heard so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So the reality is you don't know who killed Ms. Zukic or really who took the Passat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I have never said that I knew who had killed Mrs. Zukic. I only said that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you heard this before the incident on the Drina, but obviously between the time that Ms. Zukic came in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you -- when did you find out that -- from this person that believed Ms. Zukic had been killed and her Passat had been taken by Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It was between those two points in time. Now I understand your question. It was -- it was between the incident in Drina and -- yeah, in between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that the police were seizing many cars, including your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I have never said that the police took my car. It is, however, true that they were taking away some vehicles and that many vehicles that were parked outside the Visegrad Hotel had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And also many cars parked outside the police station as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I've never said that I saw vehicles parked outside the police station that were taken away. I said that I saw vehicles parked outside the Visegrad Hotel being seized. That's not where the police station was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you see seized vehicles near the police station, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is that no, that you didn't see, or no, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I really don't know what you're referring to, sir, whether I've seen vehicles parked outside the police station or whether I had seen the police officers pulling cars over by the roadside and then seizing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Had you seen that, police officers pulling cars over and seizing them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you returned to work and returned to Visegrad, were you made aware of a large gathering at the stadium of many Muslims when the Uzice Corps came into town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question truly. Maybe there had been Muslims gathered, but I wasn't in town at the time. I don't know on what date such a gathering took place. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But did you hear about it just talking amongst your countrymen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I didn't hear anyone talk of that gathering, not then at the time. I did hear that there was a gathering, but I don't know the details surrounding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you said that when you had to go -- or when you came back you had to go through five check-points?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And were these check-points manned by police, soldiers, or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: If we take it in the right order, the first one was manned by the army, the second one as well. I think only the last one at the very entrance to the town was manned by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How would you explain the relevance of all of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm explaining the overall political and command situation, also showing that the police basically controlled egress and access routes to the town. You know, there's a lot of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How does it affect the criminal responsibility of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How does it assist us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It provides tendrils to alternative theories of liability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That sounds like a refrain to which you resort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and I hope to bring it together in my final submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge van den Wyngaert will have something to say to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I just wanted to add something to this. In your effort to go over the overall situation, please keep in mind that much of this has been part of the adjudicated facts at the beginning of the decision on adjudicated facts. So let's not dwell too much on that and keep our timetable in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You did indicate though that while the Uzice Corps were in town you personally knew people who went to the police station and were not seen again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this happened despite the fact that the Uzice Corps were in town supposedly to protect Muslims, yet these people were taken by officials of the community. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And despite the fact that the Uzice Corps were in town, that's when you first noticed these paramilitary groups who you commonly called the White Eagles. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And these represented several groups, not just one group. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. Let me briefly explain this or clarify this. We believed that they would leave together with the Uzice Corps. This, however, did not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, may I interrupt you a second time. I'm just trying to understand your answer to the question of Judge Robinson, because you say explaining the overall political and command situation, et cetera, but aren't the accused only charged under Article 7(1), and so what is the relevance of this more general picture that you want to bring? You're exploring alternative modes of liability, but I'm still not -- I don't understand what you are heading for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, in the indictment, Your Honour, the Prosecution alleges that Mr. Lukic is a leader and he is a leader of the White Eagles, and you know, maybe I'm beating a dead horse, but you know, if that is part of their theory of the case, I think there's several references amongst the witnesses that can't identify him as any sort of leader much less of the White Eagles, and so I think that's kind of why I hang on this issue more and more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I would appreciate you concentrating more on the forms of liability in 7(1) as they emerge from the indictment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when Dr. Safet was in town -- or killed, the Uzice Corps were in town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I didn't say that Dr. Safet was killed at the time. He was only taken away at the time. The Uzice Corps was in town at the time, and I said that it was at the initiative of the head of the hospital and the town authorities that Safet actually returned to town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And these town authorities included the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I really don't know who was in charge of the town at the time. I didn't have even the remotest possibility of knowing who the town authorities were, who ran the town at the time. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, isn't it true, though, that -- a little later in your -- pardon me, a little later in your testimony you indicated that your friend dropped the name of Brane Savovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did mention the name of Brane Savovic, but you're asking me about matters as they were during the presence of the Uzice Corps. I said that Brane Savovic was the president of the municipality, but this was the case after the departure of the Uzice Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I understand. And he was a member of the SDS, the president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that Risto Perisic was commander of the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, so I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Dragomir Gavrilovic was also a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Savovic was put in place at the Uzice Corps' departure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I don't know when he took that position precisely, but I presume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the time that you were approach by a White Eagle to buy your head, as you stated, what -- what told you that this person was a White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how could you tell he was a White Eagles? Did he say this, or did he have some kind of uniform or way about him that indicated he was a White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I will repeat. I said that at the earlier hearing and today -- whenever in my statement I refer to the White Eagles I'm actually referring to all the paramilitaries. They were collectively referred to as the White Eagles. The two lads who approached me to buy my head, I just happened to be there. I don't know if they came to pick the vehicle -- pick up the vehicle that was there. One of them had a black beret on his head and the two --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, a red beret.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: -- with two red -- with a two-headed eagle. The other one had a green beret on his head with a two-headed eagle. I said probably they were members of the White Eagles. Now, when I asked the one with the red beret, "Where are you from," he said, "Raki, he's asking us where we're from. Shall we tell him? If I tell you where I'm from, then I have to kill you." I said, "No, no, sir. You don't have to tell me," so we were in fact joking because they were quite polite, although I had to buy my head off them. And now that you're asking me about -- of them, let me tell you one other thing. The one wearing the red beret told me, "Dear, sir, who will I have to answer to if I kill you now." I thought it over and concluded that the man was right. Who was he going to be held answerable to? But he told me, "You know, lad, I'm not a Chetnik killer. I'm a Chetnik looter." That was his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that person indicated to you that he would turn you over to the men from Obrenovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, Obrenovac. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you indicated in your statement that you believe Milan Lukic worked in Obrenovac, but what proof or information do you have of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I said I heard he worked in Obrenovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And who did you hear this from? Was it a general rumour, or did someone think they had specific knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: If I said it was common knowledge you will interpret it as a general rumour, but I knew many people who knew him personally and who told me that he worked in Obrenovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so at this point in time the name Milan Lukic was the topic of discussion amongst you and people you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you know what Milan Lukic -- was it discussed what Milan Lukic was doing in Obrenovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was it discussed the age of the person named Milan Lukic that you were discussing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It was said that it was born between '65 and '68. Some said '67. Yes, that's right. '69, perhaps. It all depends on who were the participants in the conversation and the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you attempted to leave Visegrad, you ended up having to get a permit. Is isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you were turned back at a check-point in Dobrun. Who manned that check-point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It was a police check-point. The police manned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Had you heard anywhere that people were having to pay for these permits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I really didn't hear anything of the sort, but in view of the state we were living in and the way it still functions today, it's far from impossible that people had to pay or were asked to pay. I did not pay anything myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because you had a relationship with the police officer that you met outside the police station. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: It was not a policeman. He was an employee, a clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: A clerk at the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: For a while he may have even been the commander of the station before the war. He worked on the police force. He was not an active duty policeman on the beat. When I say "employee," I don't mean to say he was a civilian person worked -- who worked in the police station. He had a desk job at the police station. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how far is Dobrun from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Twenty-six kilometres approximately. I'm not quite sure. Approximately 20, 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what was the name of this police commander who you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: His name was Ceho Mikan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And whose signature appeared on your permit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you recall the signature on your permit, the person that signed it so that you would have authority to leave Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I really don't recall, Your Honours, who signed it, but I know that my friend had to take the paper to be signed by someone. The main thing is he didn't sign it myself because he couldn't. He even had to wait for half an hour to be signed. It must have been signed by the person who was in charge of these matters, but I really can't remember who.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And moving to June 7th, you saw that your car drove by and that's what drew your attention and brought you out. Isn't that tree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And who took your car? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So was it taken from your garage, presumably, where you'd left it last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I did not keep my car in the garage. I have to emphasise that. When the men came to take the Mercedes away my car was standing outside the garage, and they told me, you have to move your car. It's not much of a car, otherwise we take it away. So I moved it to the next spot so that he can out with the Mercedes and that's where I left it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the person that took the Mercedes, is it a police officer or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I already said a moment ago and earlier today that it's the person who made me pay ransom to stay alive. I think I've explained it all today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I don't mean to belabour things, but I'm going through my notes and if I repeat -- if I repeat your testimony, I apologise. Now, after the gentlemen came and took you and you were in custody, and you left -- you said you went through a Territorial Defence check-point. It was manned by the regular Serbian army, or was it manned by local police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Could you clarify that question? Do you mean the check-point at the intersection leading to Sase?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes. That one was manned by the police. It was not an army check-point or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And those police officers allowed your -- you to proceed through with your captors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in talking about Branimir Savovic, isn't it true that the SDS is an extremist party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's probably how they were qualified, but if you say that it's an extremist party, then you have to tell it to the current SDS, which is still an active political party in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I wouldn't quite agree if we look at it from today's point of view and if we look at the SDS which still exists in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I can't call it extremist if it's sitting on the government of my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How about in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I don't know that all members of the SDS were extremists, and the man who helped me eventually may also have been a member of the SDS, but I can't say that he was an extremist. It's a very debatable question. We can spend three days on it. I really don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sir, we don't have three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But when you friend and fellow captive requested to speak with Mr. Savovic, that was because he was a leader and he thought that that could make a difference? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Sir, I explained it nicely today and the today before, and I can explain it again. The two of them were very close friends. I can similarly say that a friend of mind, that is the friend I mentioned, worked in the municipal assembly, was part of the authorities on the municipal level until a few days before the incident, and he had probably seen and met frequently with Mr. Savovic, and that's what I said. They were close friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true, though, that the only way that you knew that this person was Milan was because the other soldier told you he'd have to speak with Milan first before he could accommodate this person's requested to speak with Mr. Savovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I want to make this clear to the Honourable Court. The situation we were in at the time and the soldier guarding us in the doorway did not give us any reason to believe that he could shoot at us. He even asked my friend, as I said, do you have any children and so-and-so. We did not think of him as an executionist -- executioner, but he must have known very well what was going to happen to us. Whether I found out from him the name Milan or not would not have saved me from death at that point, so it didn't mean anything that he mentioned Milan's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir, the question I asked you though is isn't it true that that's the only reason that you knew that this masked person in a blue camouflage uniform was named Milan?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not aware of any testimony that he was wearing a mask.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, black paint, to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the only reason that you knew this person that was wearing blue camouflage with the beret with black paint obstructing his face was named Milan because the other soldier named him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer yet. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The witness again has never used the words the face was obstructed. I would ask that we remain faithful to the words of the witness if we're going to ask him to adopt them at a later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Reformulate, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was the black paint on this gentleman's face with the blue camouflage obstructing his features?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But isn't it true that the only reason you knew this person's name was Milan was because the other soldier told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was the only reason. I'd rather say it was a confirmation of everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it's also because you believed that the red Passat was there and you associate the red Passat with Milan Lukic as well. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I have said -- I said that until this moment and this talk in the house, I had never seen the red Passat before. I said that when they led us out of the house and we got outside, that's when I saw the red Passat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it was only at this time that between the one gentleman telling you the name Milan and seeing the red Passat that you believed that this is Milan Lukic who killed Behija Zukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: He didn't say that to me. The way you put your question is that the soldier told me the name. He told that to my friend, in fact. Similarly you said -- could you repeat that last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm more concerned that when you had the realisation that you believed this was Milan Lukic, and I'm telling you that isn't it true that this comes from a combination of factors, which is you heard the name Milan, and you also saw the red Passat. So putting those two factors together, you assume it's Milan Lukic who you had heard about before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's the way you interpret it. I would not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you were put into the Yugo, at first there was some discord because the soldier that sat in the back made the person in the middle sort of sit on the lap of you or squeezed you together. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the rest of the people went in this Passat; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: My friend was riding in the front seat, Ekrem was driving, Hasan Mutapcic was in the Passat. I've said already the two persons were already standing by the Passat. They got into the car and Hasan Mutapcic with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. So does this make it five people in the Yugo and five people in the Passat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: In total. Five in the Yugo and five in the Passat, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you went to the Vilina Vlas Hotel and you added the person of Mitar Vasiljevic to the equation, how was that accommodated in the seating once you left hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I explained that in great detail in the Vasiljevic trial. He left the hotel and got into the Passat too. How they squeezed themselves, all six, into the Passat is something that the witnesses -- in fact, that Mr. Vasiljevic, himself, was better placed to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I guess what I would ask you is did you notice any problems with them getting into the Passat, i.e., soldiers getting angry or yelling at people to squeeze together or something like that that you might have been aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I've said this already. As we were leaving Banja, Yugo was standing ahead of the Passat. And since I was sitting behind the driver, logically I got into the Yugo first. My back was, therefore, to the Passat, and I really couldn't see it. And sit ting in the Yugo, I couldn't see what was going on with the Passat and how they packed themselves into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But would it be fair to say that 10 people would fit much easier in this procession than 11?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: We were 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that, you're positive of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: One hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know the two other names of people from the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: No. I never learned their names, and I've always said so. I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And on the way to the Vilina Vlas, you noticed that two mosques were torched. Did that happen before or after the Uzice Corps had left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: After.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. I'm almost done. I have no further questions, Your Honour. At this time we would tender the witness statement of the 30th of September and 1st of October, 1998, which has been uploaded as 1D100-0191, the unredacted version. And we would tender the trial testimony of this witness, which has been uploaded as 1D10-0239, the trial testimony of the September 11, 2001, into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D10-0239 will become Exhibit number 1D13, and the witness statement will become Exhibit number 1D31 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one question that I have, but before I do that in the pressure to finish on the time I inadvertently forgot to ask this witness if he recognised anyone in the courtroom. Could I ask or make a motion to reopen my direct examination to do that, and of course I would not oppose Mr. Alarid having an opportunity to cross-examine on the results of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis that the Defence may ask any questions that arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, could I ask you to take a look around the courtroom and tell us whether or not you recognise anyone in this courtroom today other than myself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: The first one from the left is Mr. Lukic, and I also recognise the gentleman next to him, but the first one on the left with the red -- reddish tie is him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to use the first and last name of the person that you recognise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are you certain of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the same smirk that I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect that the witness has identified Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-32, you say that you also recognise the other person in the -- another person in the courtroom. Could you tell us the full name of the other person that you say you recognise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: That's Mr. Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where do you recognise him from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: Well, I know him. He worked as a police officer in Visegrad before the war. I have really never heard anything about him, and I have never 25 mentioned him in any of my statements. You just asked me whether I knew him, and if I said no, I don't know this man, it would be a lie, wouldn’t it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And while that's being called up, Mr. Alarid in his examination of you elicited that there was more than one Milan Lukic, given the commonness of the name, and the question I want to ask you now is that -- the question that I want to ask you now is on the protocol book, I believe you testified that there is a column where the year of birth is recorded. As soon as this exhibit comes up, I'd ask you to look in the column which -- for Milan Lukic and tell us whether or not the year of birth was recorded in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would object to this. It's unduly suggestive, leading, and otherwise the evidence speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, apparently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In my effort to replace the full book with a scanned version, apparently that's causing some confusion now. So could I ask for the time being that the full book just be returned to the witness so that the witness can look at it, and perhaps if it could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, again the same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not upholding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to once again find the entry for Milan Lukic, and can I ask you if it does tell the year of his birth, would you please point to where that's indicated and tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-32
utterances.text: I think I've said it already. When I was explaining all these columns I said, this is the name, year of birth, where he's from, address, medicard, et cetera. The year of birth indicated is 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution now calls VG-84. Ms. Maxine Marcus will be taking this witness and she's entering the courtroom now. Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, two days ago when I was working with the 360 photo programme I did not -- I had it marked for identification but did not formally tender it and it was agreed between myself and counsel that I would formally tender it a day or two later to give them an opportunity to fully examine it, so at this time I would formally tender 65 ter exhibit 175 as a public exhibit and that's the 360 programme that has photographic images from around Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit P71, Your Honours. I apologise, Your Honours, this is already on the records. It will -- MFI will become Exhibit P54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have to bring it to your attention that we are behind, and I am considering the appropriate measures to take to bring us up back to speed. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus. How long do you plan to be in your examination, Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. I will endeavour to restrict it to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the pseudonym sheet please be passed to the witness. I have it right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You've been granted protective measures by this Court for the purposes of this proceeding, and therefore will be using a pseudonym rather than your name. Can you confirm that your name and date of birth appear on the paper in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you kindly sign that paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the court officer show the pseudonym sheet to the Defence and the Chamber, and with your leave, Your Honours, I'd like to tender the pseudonym sheet into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym name sheet will be admitted as P71 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. VG-84, I have -- I'm going to provide you with a reference sheet with the assistance of the court usher which contains the names of some persons you may wish to mention during your testimony today. I'd like to ask you to kindly refrain, if possible, from using their names and, rather, to use the pseudonym that is listed on this page or the pseudonyms that are listed on this page. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. VG-84, in June of 1992, what was your age?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Just under 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What is your highest level of education?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: High school education.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you testify in the Vasiljevic case on the 8th and 9th of October of 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review that testimony in the Bosnian language before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is there anything you wish to correct from your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: There are some insignificant things. The gist of it remains the same -- remains as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Just for clarification, we're talking about your prior testimony and not your prior statement. I just want to clarify. Do you have any clarifications to make to your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today which you were asked when you testified last time, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Yes, I would state everything the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honours, pursuant to Rule 92 ter, I tender into evidence VG-84's prior testimony in the Vasiljevic case, 65 ter numbers 146 and 147 which refer to VG-84's prior testimony of 8th and 9th October, 2001, respectively, under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 146 will become exhibit number P72 and 147 will become Exhibit number P73 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: VG-84, did you give a statement to Tribunal investigators on the 20th of January, 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review that statement in the Bosnian language before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: During proofing you made a few minor clarifications to that statement. Could I kindly ask the court officer to call up 65 ter number 179 and to go to e-court page 1. VG-84, do you see the statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just for clarification, it's not being broadcast. Thank you. Is there anything you'd like to correct on the page we see on the screen in front of us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Yes. It says that I was 12 and I was just under 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the court officer please go to page 2. If we go to the fourth paragraph in the English.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Is there any clarification you would like to make to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Where it says between 10 to 15.000 persons, in fact it should say 1.000 to 1.500.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the court officer please go to e-court page 3, paragraph 4. This paragraph begins "At the end of May." VG-84, is there anything in that paragraph which you would like to correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Yes. It says Jasmina Bosno, whereas his name is Jasmina Vila. There were such similar family names in that village, so I got a bit confused. In other words, the person was Jasmina Vila.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Three paragraphs further down on that page is a paragraph beginning "On the 13th of June, 1992." Is there anything you'd like to correct in that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Well, yes. The 14th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: E-court page 4, please. The second paragraph on page 4, approximately the second line starts "He said that he was the president of the Red Cross." Is there anything in that line or the next line you wish to correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Yes. Mujo Halilovic. It says Jasarevic, and it should say Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. And the last clarification would be three paragraphs after that. Near the end of that paragraph the sentence begins "All that time we could hear." Is there anything you would like to clarify in that line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Which part is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's -- the paragraph begins "When I got to the house, I went to the middle of the basement," and the line would be a bit further near the end of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Where it says "drunken soldiers," I was giving a statement to the investigators. Whether they were there or not, I was never able to conclude with any certainty, but I definitely didn't say ever that they were drunk. There must have been some sort of misunderstanding. I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. VG-84, with those clarifications in mind, if I were to ask you the same questions today which you were asked when that statement was taken, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-84
utterances.text: Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this statement under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 179 will become P74 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I continue I'd also like to tender the underlying exhibits that were referred to in the witness's prior testimony. Those are 65 ter number 144 and 145. Those are photographs that the witness marked during his prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit P75 and Exhibit P76 respectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this might be a good time to break if you see fit to do so. Otherwise, I'm certainly happy to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much more do you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I would say about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And how long will you be, Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not quite -- to be honest, Your Honour, I'm not quite sure. Every witness is different depending on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to break now, and we will resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 5th day of September, 2008, at 8.50 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
